source.title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
source.authors: Curt Tigges; Oskar John Hollinsworth; Atticus Geiger; Neel Nanda

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies linear sentiment directions and sentiment circuits, but does not test any of the listed claims about neuron-pole job shares, explanation validation, or neuron-based attribution graphs.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a qualitative neuron analysis in Appendix A.5. Its neuron examples and cosine-similarity distribution are recorded as related findings, not as tests of the listed claim versions. Other sentiment-direction and circuit results do not measure the claim versions and are omitted.
record.test_reason: The paper studies a linear sentiment direction and attention-head circuits in GPT-2/Pythia. Its only neuron content (Appendix A.5) is four hand-picked GPT2-small neurons, taken from the tails of a cosine-similarity distribution and described anecdotally. It gives no share of neurons with one or two jobs (V1, V2). It does not touch InceptionV1 or recursive generalization (V3), or architecture versus tools (V4). It builds no neuron-based attribution graph compared against a replacement model (V5). It does not score or validate neuron explanations on held-out activations (V6, V7). It does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Sentiment is represented by a causally relevant linear direction across GPT-2 and Pythia models. Sentiment is also summarized at non-valenced tokens such as commas: ablating the direction loses 76% of above-chance SST accuracy, and 36% comes from commas alone. The neuron examples are called anecdotal. The authors suggest studying MLPs and individual neurons further, especially for negation.
record.recipe_differences: The study finds sentiment directions with methods such as clustering and DAS, then uses patching, ablation, and circuit analysis; it does not audit neuron poles or test neuron explanations on held-out activations.

fits_no_version.finding: Four GPT2-small neurons from the tails of a heavy-tailed distribution (similarity of neuron out-directions to a sentiment direction) were inspected in Neuroscope. Each is described as negation- or contrast-related. One neuron's inputs from MLP2 neurons are described as sparse.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons whose output weights align strongly with a known feature direction tend to look interpretable by activation inspection (anecdotal, GPT2-small).

record.problems: The neuron examples are qualitative and selected from the tails of a similarity distribution; they do not provide a representative sample or estimate a share of interpretable neurons. The paper notes that only a cursory human sanity check was performed for its GPT-4 token-sentiment classifications.
record.rows_left_out: Sentiment-direction and circuit results in Sections 3–4 and the appendix were left out because they do not measure any listed claim version.

untested.parts: All of it: the Qwen3-32B audit and the shares of neuron poles with one job, two jobs or not yet understood.
All of it: shares across dense and MoE models and across scale.
All of it: InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, shared pose feature, recursive generalization.
All of it: architecture, regularization and tools as the cause, and the rise in interpretable share with better tools.
All of it: neuron-based attribution graphs compared with a replacement model.
All of it: whether explanations from activating examples predict firing on unseen text.
All of it: simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not one of the original sources. Appendix A.5's heading claims sentiment-writing neurons 'are interpretable', but the evidence is four tail-selected examples. It cannot inform shares of interpretable neurons.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit, neuron-pole job proportions, and validation on activations not used to write explanations.
Shares across dense and mixture-of-experts models and scaling up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, shared pose feature, and recursive generalization.
Architecture, regularization, tool quality, and the stated estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and comparison with a trained replacement model and its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict firing on unseen examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: GPT2-small
rows.operation_detail: Inspected a high-similarity neuron's activations and traced its contribution through the network.

conditions.value: “I would not hesitate” vs. “I would always hesitate”

rows.measure: Qualitative activation pattern and attribution analysis
rows.value: The neuron is described as activating on “hesitate” following a negation; the analysis identifies L1H0, L3H10, L3H11, and MLP2 as main contributors to the difference between the two example prompts.
rows.note: The authors present this as an extended, anecdotal example, not as a representative neuron sample.
rows.check: This is a single hand-selected neuron, described anecdotally. 'Observed' only means the description exists; it does not show any version's effect, so the state is changed to cannot_determine. The 'numbers_found 2/2' entry is unclear.
